blocks.content: The previous topic covered what a table, row, and column actually are, this topic covers the specific column, or set of columns, that uniquely identifies each individual row, the primary key, a concept every well designed table depends on.

This topic covers exactly what a primary key guarantees, the tradeoff between using a natural value like an email address versus a generated surrogate id, and why a stable primary key matters so much once other tables start referencing it.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784643745362-183658601.png
blocks.alt: Building on tables, rows, and columns, the primary key uniquely identifies each row

blocks.content: 1. What a Primary Key Guarantees

A primary key is a column, or combination of columns, whose value is guaranteed to be unique across every row in the table, and never null, this guarantee is enforced directly by the database, not just a convention a team happens to follow.
Suppose your customers table has an id column declared as the primary key, the database itself will reject any attempt to insert a second row with an id value that already exists.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784643747272-934350438.png
blocks.alt: Rows with id 1, 2, and 3 are accepted, a duplicate id 1 is rejected outright

blocks.content: 2. Why Unique Identification Actually Matters
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784643748854-488333552.png
blocks.alt: Without a primary key it is unclear which row is which, with one, exactly one row is identified

blocks.content: Without a reliable way to identify exactly one row, updating or deleting a specific customer record becomes genuinely ambiguous, if two rows happen to share every column value, which one do you actually mean to update, a primary key removes this ambiguity entirely.

{"headers":["Without a Primary Key","With a Primary Key"],"rows":[["Rows may be indistinguishable from each other","Every row has a value that uniquely identifies it"],["Updating one specific row is ambiguous","A single primary key value targets exactly one row"]]}
3. Natural Keys vs Surrogate Keys
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784643750396-76246203.png
blocks.alt: A natural key like email is compared against a surrogate key like an auto incrementing id

blocks.content: A natural key uses an attribute that already has real world meaning, an email address or a national id number, a surrogate key instead uses a value generated purely for identification purposes, most commonly an auto incrementing integer, with no meaning outside the database itself.
A worked example choosing between the two

4. How Auto Incrementing Surrogate Keys Work
blocks.text: 4. How Auto Incrementing Surrogate Keys Work

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784643751914-837748018.png
blocks.alt: Each inserted row gets an automatically assigned id, and the next insert receives the next id

blocks.content: When a surrogate key column is declared auto incrementing, the database assigns the next available integer value automatically on every insert, the application code never needs to manually track or generate the next id value itself.
5. Why NULL Is Never Allowed
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784643753412-220377921.png
blocks.alt: An attempt to insert a NULL primary key value is rejected by the database

blocks.content: A primary key value can never be null, a null value would mean a row has no identity at all, defeating the entire purpose of a primary key, the database enforces this restriction automatically alongside the uniqueness guarantee.

blocks.title: Uniqueness and NOT NULL together are what define a primary key
blocks.content: A column can be declared UNIQUE without being the primary key, and still allow nulls in some databases, a true primary key specifically combines uniqueness with a strict NOT NULL requirement.
6. Why Stability Matters Once Other Tables Reference It
blocks.text: 6. Why Stability Matters Once Other Tables Reference It

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784643755123-60235963.png
blocks.alt: An orders table primary key, order_id, gets referenced by other tables

blocks.content: Once other tables start referencing a primary key value, covered in depth in the next Foreign Key topic, that value needs to remain stable over time, if a customer email primary key changes when they update their email address, every table referencing that old email value now points to an outdated identifier.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784643756667-760961766.png
blocks.alt: An email value can change over time while a surrogate id never changes

blocks.content: 7. When a Natural Key Is Still a Reasonable Choice
blocks.text: 7. When a Natural Key Is Still a Reasonable Choice

blocks.content: A natural key can still be a reasonable choice for a value that is both genuinely unique and genuinely stable, a country code or a well governed product SKU for instance, the deciding factor is whether the value could ever legitimately need to change, if it could, a surrogate key avoids that entire class of problem.

blocks.title: Surrogate keys are the more common default in practice
blocks.content: Most production schemas default to a surrogate integer id specifically because it sidesteps the risk of a natural value changing later, even when a natural key looks unique and stable today.
8. Common Mistakes

["Choosing a natural key value that could plausibly change later, like an email address or phone number","Assuming a UNIQUE constraint alone is equivalent to a primary key, without the strict NOT NULL guarantee","Not declaring any primary key at all, leaving rows with no reliable way to be uniquely identified","Manually generating id values in application code instead of relying on the database auto increment feature"]
items: Choosing a natural key value that could plausibly change later, like an email address or phone number
Assuming a UNIQUE constraint alone is equivalent to a primary key, without the strict NOT NULL guarantee
Not declaring any primary key at all, leaving rows with no reliable way to be uniquely identified
Manually generating id values in application code instead of relying on the database auto increment feature

blocks.content: 9. Key Takeaways

["A primary key uniquely identifies every row and can never be null, enforced directly by the database","A surrogate key, typically an auto incrementing integer, avoids the instability risk a natural key like an email address carries","Primary key stability matters enormously once other tables begin referencing it as a foreign key","The next topic, Foreign Key, covers exactly how one table references another table primary key"]
items: A primary key uniquely identifies every row and can never be null, enforced directly by the database
A surrogate key, typically an auto incrementing integer, avoids the instability risk a natural key like an email address carries
Primary key stability matters enormously once other tables begin referencing it as a foreign key
The next topic, Foreign Key, covers exactly how one table references another table primary key
